senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: the quality of holiness as an expression of the divine in contrast with the human
the state resulting from being dedicated to the service of God
pertaining to the absence of yeast
senses.comment: The phrase ‘unleavened bread’ may be rendered as ‘bread made without yeast’ or ‘bread which does not rise.’ Perhaps a more difficult problem is involved in the relationship of ‘days’ to ‘unleavened bread,’ and accordingly, the expression ‘the days of Unleavened Bread’ may be rendered as ‘the days when people ate bread that had no yeast.’ Except for 1 Corinthians 5:7, in which ἄζυμος occurs in a highly figurative passage referring to pure and true life, this term is used exclusively in reference to the feast or festival of Unleavened Bread.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being without fault and hence guileless
senses.comment: In Hebrews 7:26 ἄκακος has a far more positive meaning than merely not being bad. In other words, the negation of κακός[a] bad (88.106) does not produce a term which is merely morally neutral, but it designates something of a clearly positive character.

senses.def: pertaining to being unsuspecting or naive with regard to possible deception
senses.comment: It may be possible to spell out the implications of ἄκακος in Romans 16:18 by translating ‘the minds of people who do not suspect lies.’

senses.def: to employ an analogy or likeness in communicating

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to not being subject to blame and hence morally irreproachable
glosses: being one who cannot be blamed

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being without guilt
pertaining to what cannot be criticized
senses.comment: It may be necessary in some languages to restructure ἀκατάγνωστος and ἀνεπίλημπτος as complete clauses, so that instead of ‘sound words which are above criticism’ in Titus 2:8, one may translate ‘sound words which no one can criticize’ or ‘… against which no one can say anything.’ ‘Above reproach’ in 1 Timothy 6:14 may be rendered as ‘in such a way that no one can criticize it.’

senses.def: a city in Syria
a city in Pisidia
to cause to move away from a point by threat or by force
senses.comment: A strictly literal translation of Acts 18:16 as ‘he drove them out of court’ might imply that Gallio personally and physically forced them out of the court; probably, he simply caused them to be driven out of the court by court officials. Therefore, it may be necessary in some languages to indicate this causative relationship by ‘he ordered them to leave the court’ or ‘he ordered the officials to force them out of the court.’

senses.def: the Greek name for the ruling angel in Hell; see 93.2
a person in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:3; Luke 3:33, apparatus)
the head shepherd who directs the activities of other shepherds (in its only NT occurrence; a figurative reference to Christ)

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of ἀτακτέω ‘to do nothing,’ 88.246) pertaining to refusing to work

senses.subdomain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
senses.def: (derivative of ἀφρίζω ‘to cause foaming of a liquid,’ 14.28) a frothy, foaming mass or substance
senses.comment: Though ἀφρός may refer to any type of foam or frothy substance, in Luke 9:39 the reference is clearly to frothy saliva coming out of the mouth, something which is typical of persons experiencing an epileptic seizure. A number of languages have quite specific terms for this type of foaming or frothing at the mouth, expressed literally in some instances as ‘his saliva was bubbling out of his mouth’ or ‘the water of his mouth came out in bubbles.’

senses.def: to bear or carry a relatively heavy or burdensome object
to carry away from a place, with the probable implication of something that is relatively heavy
(similar in meaning to ὑποφέρω ‘to endure,’ 25.175, but probably somewhat more emphatic in meaning) to continue to bear up under unusually trying circumstances and difficulties
to provide continuous and possibly prolonged assistance and help by supplying the needs of someone
to undergo a grievous, difficult experience
to accept, but with the implication of the truth being difficult to comprehend or to respond to properly
(an idiom, literally: to carry a name) to spread information extensively about a person
(an idiom, literally: to bear marks) to undergo experiences which mark one as the slave of some master
glosses: to bear the marks of a slave
to experience being the slave of
senses.comment: See also 8.55 and 33.481.

senses.def: (a productive idiomatic expression, literally: to carry one’s cross) to be prepared to endure severe suffering, even to the point of death
glosses: to be prepared to suffer even unto death
senses.comment: The idiom ‘to carry one’s cross’ or ‘to take up one’s cross’ involves a number of important features of meaning. Unfortunately, this expression is frequently not understood correctly by many people who hear it or even use it. One reason for this is the actual absence of crucifixion in modern society. If a literal translation is to be employed, then some marginal note will probably be necessary in order to indicate clearly the full implications of such a statement.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: the womb carries) to experience the process of pregnancy
senses.comment: It may, however, be necessary in some languages to render Luke 11:27 as ‘fortunate is the woman who gave you birth,’ since a literal reference to carrying in the womb may seem unduly crude.

senses.def: to cry or shout with unusually loud volume
(derivative of Γαλιλαία ‘Galilee,’ 93.444) a person who is a native of Galilee
(derivative of γέμω ‘to be laden,’ not occurring in the NT) a relatively heavy object which is carried
cardinal number, where there are fifteen instances of a countable entity
to divide and distribute to persons on the basis of certain implied distinctions or differences
to carry or take something through an area or structure
to cause to move in various directions by means of a force
to be different from someone or something
to be of considerable value, in view of having certain distinctive characteristics
to filter or strain out substances from a liquid

senses.subdomain: Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
senses.def: the twelve tribes of Israel as a designation of the entire ethnic unit
a temple or sanctuary which houses an idol
senses.comment: The term εἰδωλεῖον may be rendered as ‘the building in which an idol is placed’ or ‘a large house in which an idol is worshiped.’ Since ‘idol’ is often rendered as ‘the statue of a god,’ εἰδωλεῖον may be rendered as ‘the building in which there is a statue of a god’ or ‘a building in which a statue of a god is worshiped.’

senses.def: to exert considerable effort and care in learning something
to charge someone with a crime or offense
to cause someone to become terrified or very much afraid

senses.subdomain: Processes Involving the Mouth, Other Than Eating and Drinking
senses.comment: Since a term meaning ‘to vomit’ often carries somewhat vulgar connotations, ἐμέω in Revelation 3:16 has frequently been translated as ‘to spit out of my mouth.’|It is also possible to interpret ‘to vomit out of the mouth’ as an idiom meaning ‘to reject.’

senses.def: to be engaged in some activity or function, with possible focus upon the energy or force involved
to cause or make possible a particular function
glosses: to grant the ability to do
senses.comment: In many instances it is important to specify the references of πάντα and πᾶσιν in 1 Corinthians 12:6, so that one may translate ‘the same God gives the ability to everyone for his or her particular service.’

senses.def: to cause a state to be

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to an extremely short period of time between a previous state or event and a subsequent state or event
senses.comment: In a number of contexts there is the implication of unexpectedness; but this seems to be a derivative of the context as a whole and not a part of the meaning of the lexical items.

senses.def: to cause something to be or to become correct, with the implication of a previous condition of faults or failures
(a technical, nautical term) to cause a ship to run up onto or against a shore
senses.comment: In some instances it may be necessary to translate ἐπικέλλω as ‘they caused the ship to get stuck in the sand’ or ‘… in the mud.’

senses.def: to place something on something
to add something to an existing quantity
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is not at all difficult to speak of ‘adding things,’ but to add events may provide some special difficulties in restructuring. For example, in Luke 3:20 it may be important to translate as ‘he had done many other bad things, but he also did this,’ and in Galatians 2:6 it may be helpful to translate ‘for those who were of repute did not say that I should do anything more than I was doing.’

senses.def: to subject someone to a particular experience, normally by the use of force
senses.comment: In Revelation 22:18, there is obviously a play on two different meanings of ἐπιτίθημι, ‘to add to’ and ‘to subject to.’ In the preceding clause ἐάν τις ἐπιθῇ ἐπ̓ αὐτά, the meaning is clearly ‘if anyone adds to these’ (see ἐπιτίθημι[b], 59.72), but in the second clause there is both the addition as well as the subjection of a person to punishment.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to put a yoke upon the neck) to cause difficulty to someone by requiring conformity to rules and regulations
glosses: to place a burden on the backs of

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to place a name) to give a name to, with the possible implication of an additional name
to place something at the disposal of someone else
to use sudden physical force against someone as the outgrowth of a hostile attitude
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to attack’ is simply ‘to start fighting against.’ In some languages, however, the equivalent is ‘to jump on’ or ‘to grab to do harm to.’

senses.def: a position defined as being within certain limits

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἔσω ‘inside,’ 83.13) a person belonging to a so-called in-group (in other words, not being a member of the out-group in question)
senses.comment: See also 11.10.|In the rendering of 1 Corinthians 5:12 it may be necessary to be quite specific about those who constitute outsiders and insiders, for example, ‘why should I judge those who are not believers? should you not judge the believers?’ Note the rendering of TEV for 1 Corinthians 5:12: “After all, it is none of my business to judge outsiders. God will judge them. But should you not judge the members of your own fellowship? As the scripture says, ‘Remove the evil man from your group.’ ”

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: the inner (person)) the psychological faculty, including intellectual, emotional, and spiritual aspects, in contrast with the purely physical aspects of human existence
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is quite impossible to speak of the psychological faculty of a person as being merely ‘that which is within.’ It is frequently necessary to refer to a particular organ of the body, for example, ‘the heart’ or ‘the liver’ or ‘the spleen.’ In some languages, however, one may refer to this faculty as being ‘the person who stands inside’ or ‘the real person’ or even ‘the other person.’|In Luke 17:21 the phrase ἐντὸς ὑμῶν in the statement ἰδοὺ γὰρ ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ἐντὸς ὑμῶν ἐστιν ‘look, God’s reign is within you’ may constitute a reference to the same inner being designated by the phrases ὁ ἔσω and ὁ ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ. On this basis some scholars have suggested that the phrase ἐντὸς ὑμῶν can be interpreted as a potentiality for participation and hence be translated ‘within your grasp,’ but it is more likely that one should understand the phrase ἐντὸς ὑμῶν in Luke 17:21 as a spacial relationship, for example, ‘in your midst’ or ‘among you’ (see 83.9).

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: doing that which is good and beneficial to someone

senses.subdomain: Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
senses.def: to be deeply committed to something, with the implication of accompanying desire
to produce a sound or noise not involving human speech
senses.comment: In translating χαλκὸς ἠχῶν it is usually desirable to employ a term which will more specifically refer to the sound of brass cymbals, for example, ‘resounding cymbal’ or ‘clanging cymbal.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: echoing brass, or: resounding brass) a gong made of brass
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of gong is ‘noisy metal’ or ‘reverberating metal’ or ‘echoing metal,’ but frequently translators have simply used an expression meaning ‘loud bell.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of θηριομαχέω ‘to be forced to fight with wild animals,’ not occurring in the NT) to be in conflict with forceful opposition
glosses: to be in a serious struggle with
senses.comment: Some persons have assumed that θηριομαχέω in 1 Corinthians 15:32 is to be understood in a literal sense, but this is very unlikely. One can, however, preserve something of the figurative force of this expression by rendering this question in 1 Corinthians 15:32 as “if I have, as it were, fought ‘wild beasts’ here in Ephesus simply from human motives, what have I gained?” (TEV). By making a metaphor into a simile one can preserve something of the figurative value of the phrase, while at the same time not introducing possible misunderstanding.

senses.def: the role of being a priest
(derivative of Ἰσραήλ[b], 93.182) the ethnic name of a person belonging to the nation of Israel
an emphatic marker of comparison between events and states
to move down, irrespective of the gradient
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is a series of terms for going down or descending, depending upon the gradient and the rapidity with which someone or something descends. There may also be distinct terms depending upon the extent of the descent. Rain coming down would be regarded as an extensive descent, while getting out of a boat to walk on the water would be a very limited descent.|Movement downward may, of course, involve more than physical objects, for example, οὐκ ἔστιν αὕτη ἡ σοφία ἄνωθεν κατερχομένη ‘this is not the wisdom that comes down from above’ James 3:15. Since in James 3:15 ἄνωθεν is a substitute for God, it may be necessary to restructure this statement as ‘this wisdom does not come from God’ or ‘God is not the source of this wisdom.’

senses.def: to move toward and to arrive at a point
to attain or arrive at a particular state
to happen to, with the implication of something definitive and final
to prevent someone from doing something by restraining or hindering
to continue to believe, with the implication of acting in accordance with such belief
glosses: to continue to believe and practice

senses.def: to have or possess objects or property (in the technical sense of having control over the use of such objects)
to exercise continuous control over someone or something
senses.comment: There is usually no difficulty in speaking of ‘control’ if it is performed by a person as in 1 Peter 2:13. However, it may not be possible to speak of ‘death’ having control, unless the language in question can personify death. In some instances Acts 2:24 (see 37.16) must be rendered as ‘it was impossible for him to continue to be dead,’ and in 2 Corinthians 5:14 ‘Christ’s love controls us’ may be rendered as ‘the fact that Christ loves us causes us to act as we do.’

senses.def: to come to occupy a particular place
glosses: to come to be in a place

senses.def: (a nautical idiom, literally: to control toward) to control the movement of a ship to a particular point
(derivative of κοινωνέω[a] ‘to share,’ 57.98) pertaining to willing and ready sharing
the sound of a loud scream or shout
to weep or wail, with emphasis upon the noise accompanying the weeping
a city that had the status of a κώμη (1.92) as far as its legal standing or constitution was concerned
the aromatic resin of certain trees, burned for its pleasing aroma
senses.comment: Translators may either borrow a term such as ‘frankincense’ or use a descriptive equivalent, for example, ‘a sweet-smelling incense’ or ‘a valuable, sweet incense.’

senses.def: pertaining to being useless on the basis of being futile and lacking in content
a marker of an associative relation, usually with the implication of being in the company of
a marker of association, involving instruments relevant to an event
a marker of a relation in which one thing is combined with another
senses.comment: This expression in Luke 13:1 must be understood in a figurative sense, for it refers to the act of Pilate killing the people while they were sacrificing.|In some languages this expression in Ephesians 6:23 can only be expressed as ‘love and trust at the same time.’ |In 1 Timothy 2:15 modesty is in a combinative relation with faith, love, and holiness and not merely with holiness. In languages in which such expressions are normally translated by verbs, one may render the final clause of 1 Timothy 2:15 as ‘if she continues to trust and love and to be holy while at the same time showing modesty.’

senses.def: a marker of circumstances which contribute significantly to the context of the principal event
a marker of the experiencer of an event, with the added implication of association
(with the genitive) a marker of opposition and conflict, implying interaction

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a marker of a point of time closely associated with a prior point of time
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no convenient preposition-like word such as ‘after,’ but one can render the expression in John 3:22 as ‘these things happened, and then Jesus and his disciples went to the province of Judea.’

senses.def: a position within an area determined by other objects and distributed among such objects

senses.subdomain: Beyond, On the Other Side Of
senses.def: (with the genitive) a position farther away and behind some object
a marker of association in which one party acts or exists for the benefit of another
senses.comment: In Matthew 12:30 there is an implied event.

senses.def: a marker of means, with the probable additional implication of attendant circumstance (see μετά[d] ‘with,’ 89.79)
senses.comment: In Acts 2:28 πρόσωπον is a figurative designation for the presence of a person (see 85.26).

senses.def: a seaport city on the west coast of Asia Minor
(a figurative extension of meaning of μυωπάζω ‘to be shortsighted,’ not occurring in the NT) to be extremely limited in one’s understanding
a member of the Sanhedrin who spoke with Jesus
(derivative of ὁδηγέω[a] ‘to guide,’ 15.182) one who guides
one who guides or leads
senses.comment: In Romans 2:19 the context is figurative in the sense that ‘the blind’ are those who are spiritually blind, and the guidance which they require is a proper understanding of the truth in terms of how they should behave.

senses.def: to experience a yearning affection for someone
glosses: to have a great affection for
to have a yearning love for
senses.comment: The nominal phrase with the English term ‘affection’ can and must be expressed in a number of languages by verb phrases or clauses. In 1 Thessalonians 2:8 one may translate ‘because we love you so much, we were ready to share with you.’

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: (derivative of ὄρθρος[a] ‘early morning,’ 67.187) to get up early in the morning and go about one’s affairs
glosses: to get up early and go

senses.def: that which ought to be if one only had one’s wish
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be preferable to translate ὄφελον as simply an expression of wishing. Therefore, 2 Corinthians 11:1 might be rendered as ‘I wish you would grant me a bit of foolishness’ or ‘I wish you would tolerate a bit of foolishness on my part.’

senses.def: (derivative of παραγγέλλω ‘to order, to command,’ 33.327) an announcement as to what must be done
to serve, with the probable implication of continuity and regularity of the service
to submit to authority or reason by obeying
a particular portion or unit of discourse
senses.comment: In rendering τόπος[b], περιοχή, or γραφή[a], it is often possible to use a rather general term such as the place or the part. In other instances one may wish to use a term meaning the words. Accordingly, Luke 4:21 may be rendered as ‘these words have come true today as you have heard them being read.’

senses.def: (derivative of πιστεύω[b] ‘to trust,’ 31.85) pertaining to trusting
(derivative of πιστεύω[b] ‘to trust,’ 31.85) pertaining to being trusted
senses.comment: Since πιστός[b] is a type of passive derivative of πιστεύω[b], it may be necessary in a number of languages to render this passive relationship in an active form. For example, the phrase δοῦλε ἀγαθὲ καὶ πιστέ in Matthew 25:21 may be rendered as ‘good servant and one whom I can trust.’ In 2 Timothy 2:11 the phrase πιστὸς ὁ λόγος may be rendered as ‘this is a saying we can have confidence in’ or ‘… that we can trust.’

senses.def: pertaining to being sure, with the implication of being fully trustworthy
(derivative of πιστεύω[c] ‘to be a believer,’ 31.102) one (female) who believes in Jesus Christ

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: one (female) who is included among the faithful followers of Christ
act of engaging in open warfare
(figurative extension of meaning of πόλεμος[a] ‘war,’ 55.5) act of engaging in serious and protracted conflict, often involving a series of attacks
to carry out some activity (with possible focus upon the procedures involved)
to collect what is due (normally in terms of taxes and interest), with the possible implication of extortion (as in Luke 3:13)
to experience events and to also engage in them
to state with assurance what is to happen in the future
pertaining to a state of hunger
to cause something to be in the shape of a roll
the underground part of a plant
senses.comment: In Mark 11:20, a literal translation of ‘withered away to the roots’ may be misunderstood, since the expression might suggest that the tree had withered only as far down as the roots but that the roots had not withered. The Greek text, however, indicates that the entire tree including the roots had withered and was completely dead.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ῥίζα[a] ‘root,’ 3.47) a descendant, with probable connotations of continuing relation
(a figurative extension of meaning of ῥίζα[a] ‘root,’ 3.47) that which constitutes a basic source or reason for an event or state
senses.comment: In a number of languages this passage in 1 Timothy 6:10 must be structurally modified, for example, ‘because people love money, they do all those bad things.’

senses.subdomain: Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
senses.def: carnelian or cornelian, usually red in color (see 2.29)
pertaining to being well fed on grain and hence fattened

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to indulge oneself excessively in satisfying one’s own appetites and desires
the materials of which the world and the universe are composed
senses.comment: In many languages the closest equivalent of στοιχεῖα is ‘the things of which the world is made’ or ‘what the world is made of’ or ‘the substances of which the universe consists.’

senses.def: the supernatural powers or forces regarded as having control over the events of this world
glosses: the supernatural powers over this world
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no way of speaking of ‘supernatural powers’ or ‘supernatural forces.’ Reference can only be made to such powers in terms of kinds of spirit beings; therefore, one may render στοιχεῖα[b] in Colossians 2:20 as ‘those spirits that have power’ or ‘those spirits which control.’

senses.subdomain: Basic Principles or Features Defining the Nature of Something
senses.def: basic principles which underlie the nature of something
senses.comment: In some languages it may be extremely difficult to find the lexical equivalents of ‘the basic principles about the elementary aspects.’ In Greek this represents highly generic vocabulary, and in many languages the closest equivalent is ‘how to understand the simple truths.’ Therefore, this expression in Hebrews 5:12 may be rendered as ‘again you have need for someone to teach you how to understand the simple truths about God’s message.’

senses.def: the fruit of the fig tree
senses.comment: As in the case of the corresponding term for the fig tree (3.5), it may be best to borrow a term for fig and add a classifier, for example, ‘fruit called fig.’

senses.def: to accompany in going up to
glosses: to go or come up together with

senses.def: to break or shatter a solid object into pieces, with the implication of destruction
to cause damage to an object by crushing
senses.comment: It is difficult to know precisely what the reference is in the use of συντρίβω in Luke 9:39. The obvious result is severe pain, but it is not possible to tell precisely what symptoms are involved in what is described as being crushed by the demon.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of συντρίβω[b] ‘to crush,’ 19.46) to overcome, with the resulting crushing of the power of the opposition
a detachment of four soldiers
cardinal number, where there are three hundred instances of a countable entity
an immediate male offspring

senses.subdomain: Persons For Whom There Is Affectionate Concern
senses.def: (extension of meaning of υἱός[a] ‘son,’ 10.42) a person of any age for whom there is a special relationship of endearment and association
senses.comment: The usage of υἱός in Hebrews 12:5 reflects the relationship between a spiritual father or teacher and a follower.

senses.def: (an extended meaning of υἱός[a] ‘son,’ 10.42) a non-immediate male descendant (possibly involving a gap of several generations)
senses.comment: Though υἱός[c] is often translated as ‘son,’ speaking, for example, of ‘Joseph son of David,’ this may be very misleading in some languages, since readers would assume that a ‘son’ belonged to an immediately following generation. In some instances a term such as ‘great grandson’ is generalized to mean any individual in the third or in any one of a number of succeeding generations. In place of a phrase such as ‘descendant of David,’ it is sometimes necessary to invert the expression to read ‘David was one of his ancestors.’

senses.def: the male offspring of an animal (occurring in the NT only with ὑποζύγιον ‘beast of burden,’ 4.7)
senses.comment: See the discussion of Matthew 21:5 in 4.7.

senses.def: (followed by the genitive of class or kind) a person of a class or kind, specified by the following genitive construction
senses.comment: For a discussion of υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, see 12.15.|In most languages it is difficult, if not impossible, to represent adequately the meaning of such expressions consisting of the formula ‘son of …’ without making some significant adjustments. For example, ‘your sons’ in Matthew 12:27 may be rendered as ‘your followers.’ In Acts 13:10 ‘son of the Devil’ may be rendered as ‘you are like the Devil,’ while in Luke 16:8 ‘sons of this age’ may be readily translated as ‘people who are typical of this age.’ In Matthew 23:15 ‘son of Gehenna’ may be rendered as ‘you who deserve to go to hell,’ and in Mark 3:17 ‘sons of thunder’ may be rendered as ‘men who are like thunder’ or ‘thunderous persons.’ For idiomatic expressions involving ‘sons of …,’ see 11.13, 11.14, and 11.16.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of υἱός[a] ‘son,’ 10.42) one who is a disciple or follower of someone, with the implication of being like the one whom he follows (a reflection of the Semitic use of υἱός in the expression son of)
senses.comment: In 1 Peter 5:13 the meaning of the expression Μᾶρκος ὁ υἱός μου, literally ‘Mark, my son,’ may be ‘Mark, my disciple’ or ‘Mark, my follower.’ On the other hand, υἱός may simply be a means of referring to a younger person in an affectionate manner (see 9.46).

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a member of a sociopolitical group with some presumed ethnic relationship
a kind or class of persons, with the implication of possessing certain derived characteristics
glosses: one who has the characteristics of

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: sons of Israel) the people of Israel as an ethnic entity
senses.comment: In translating the expression ‘the people of Israel’ it may be necessary to use an appositional phrase, for example, ‘the people, namely, Israel’ or a relative clause which also serves an appositional function, for example, ‘the people who are Israel.’ In some languages it may be preferable to use a term such as ‘nation’ followed by some expression which will indicate that Israel is simply the name of the nation, for example, ‘the nation called Israel.’

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: sons of the kingdom) people who should properly be or were traditionally regarded as a part of the kingdom of God
senses.comment: In a number of languages a literal rendering of ‘sons of the kingdom’ would be relatively meaningless. It is normally possible to use a descriptive phrase in contexts such as Matthew 8:12, for example, ‘those who should be a part of the kingdom of God’ or ‘those over whom God should be ruling.’ In this context, as well as in most others, the Greek term traditionally rendered ‘kingdom’ (in speaking of ‘the kingdom of God’) points essentially to the rule of God rather than to any place or time. See also 37.64.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: sons of this age) persons who hold to the value system of the world
senses.comment: In some instances ‘the people of this world’ may be rendered as ‘the people who live like most people in the world’ or ‘the people who are concerned only about what people say.’ Sometimes the identification with the world is expressed in contrast with people’s attitude concerning God, for example, ‘people who have no use for God.’

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: sons of the wedding hall) guests at a wedding, or more specifically, friends of the bridegroom participating in wedding festivities
glosses: wedding guests or friends of the bridegroom
senses.comment: A literal rendering of the idiom ‘sons of the wedding hall’ has often been seriously misunderstood, for example, the bride’s children born prior to the marriage.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (idioms, literally: sons of the light, and: sons of the day) persons to whom the truth of God has been revealed and who are presumably living according to such truth. See also 9.4 and 12.15
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is difficult to speak of ‘light’ in the metaphorical sense of the truth that comes from God. Such truth is not to be equated with knowledge, but with the principles and practices of right moral behavior. Because of these difficulties in speaking of ‘truth’ as ‘light,’ a number of translators have preferred to use the expression ‘people of God’ for the phrases υἱοὶ τοῦ φωτός, υἱοὶ τῆς ἡμέρας, and τέκνα φωτός. In some instances, however, it is possible to employ ‘light,’ if this is described as ‘light that comes from God’ or even ‘the true light from God.’|Though there are two expressions, υἱοὶ φωτός and υἱοὶ ἡμέρας, in 1 Thessalonians 5:5, there does not seem to be any significant difference in meaning. The two phrases simply supplement and reinforce each other.

senses.def: (a Semitic idiom, literally: sons of men) human beings (equivalent in denotative meaning to ἄνθρωπος[a], 9.1)
senses.comment: It is rare indeed that one can reproduce literally the Semitic phrase ‘sons of men,’ since the expression is likely to be interpreted as relating only to the male offspring of fathers.

senses.def: a title with Messianic implications used by Jesus concerning himself
senses.comment: This title ‘Son of Man’ served not only to affirm but also to hide Christ’s Messianic role.|In a number of languages there are serious complications involved in a literal translation of υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ‘Son of Man.’ In the first place, this is likely to be understood in a more or less literal sense of ‘son of a man’ and thus a denial of the virgin birth. Such is particularly true in languages which have two words for ‘son,’ one meaning ‘son of a man’ and the other, ‘son of a woman.’ Under such circumstances, a literal translation would be a clear denial of the virgin birth.

senses.def: (a title applied to Jesus, literally: son of God; parallel in semantic structure to phrases consisting of υἱός followed by the genitive of class or kind; compare 9.4) one who has the essential characteristics and nature of God
senses.comment: Before adopting a translation of υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ such as ‘Son of God,’ one must always investigate the extent to which such an expression might already be used in a particular language. For example, in the Tarahumara language of Mexico mankind is divided into two classes: (1) ‘sons of God,’ who are Tarahumaras and (2) ‘sons of the devil,’ all other people. In these circumstances it is necessary in translating υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ to use an expression which will identify ‘the unique Son of God’ or ‘the one who is truly the Son of God.’

senses.def: a title applied to Jesus, with Messianic implications, emphasizing Jesus’ link to David

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of ὑποκρίνομαι ‘to pretend,’ 88.227) one who pretends to be other than he really is
to speak about something with certainty
a state of severe distress, aroused by intense concern for impending pain, danger, evil, etc., or possibly by the illusion of such circumstances
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no noun-like word for ‘fear.’ Accordingly, expressions containing such a noun in Greek must often be restructured so that the corresponding semantic unit may be expressed by a verb. Therefore, instead of ‘fear,’ one may have expressions such as ‘be afraid’ or ‘to fear.’ Instead of ‘fears within’ (2 Corinthians 7:5), one may translate ‘in our hearts we were afraid.’

senses.def: the occasion or source of fear
senses.comment: φόβος in the sense of ‘source of fear’ is essentially a causative, so that Romans 13:3 may often be rendered as ‘for the rulers do not cause those who do good to fear but cause those who do what is bad to fear.’

senses.def: profound respect and awe for deity
pertaining to that which causes trouble and hardship, with an implication of violence
senses.comment: It may be very difficult in some languages to speak of ‘troublous times,’ for ‘trouble’ seems to relate to human experience and not to circumstances. Therefore, this expression in 2 Timothy 3:1 can perhaps be best rendered in some languages as ‘in the last days, people will suffer very much.’

senses.def: pertaining to one who is inclined to violent and dangerous activity
that which should be or happen, with the implication of propriety
to rub something under pressure to make it smaller
senses.comment: By rubbing the heads of wheat, the disciples were able to remove the chaff and the so-called ‘beards,’ the stiff projections arising from each kernel. This process would be equivalent to threshing and would thus be condemned by the Pharisees as work on the Sabbath.
